newsitem.title: GHANA: Ghana government delays irritate opposition.
newsitem.headline: Ghana government delays irritate opposition.

text.p: Almost four months after Jerry Rawlings became Ghana's first president to win re-election, he has yet to complete the formation of his government team -- much to the irritation of the opposition.

New names have been put to parliament in batches or dribs and drabs since February 10, ministers from his previous administration are acting as caretakers in certain posts and on Friday there was a minor reshuffle of those already serving.
Some ministers have already been approved by the new parliament's vetting commission, others are yet to be vetted.
"It is absolutely chaotic," the minority leader in parliament, Joseph Henry Mensah, told Reuters last week. "I don't know any more who is minister of what.
Mensah says Rawlings, who twice seized power in the West African nation, has appointed too many ministers of state without portfolio -- currently there are seven.

"Castle watchers" -- the Castle is Ghana's seat of government -- say the main reason for the confusion and delay is that Rawlings is under pressure from the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank to trim the size of his administration.
The outgoing administration included 83 ministers and deputy ministers. Political sources say Rawlings is also under pressure to make fresh political nominations as thanks for his re-election.
"I don't know what is going on behind the scenes," said Kofi Awoonor, one of the ministers without portfolio. "It is entirely up to the president as to what ministry he will assign me."
A further reason for the delay was a rumpus in the new parliament, where Rawlings supporters have a majority, over whether it should vet ministers from his last administration.

Elected like Rawlings on December 7, the new parliament includes far more opposition members than the outgoing assembly. The main opposition boycotted the 1992 parliamentary poll after contesting Rawlings's presidential victory a month earlier.
Parliament decided on February 14, during an opposition walkout, that ministers from the previous administration do not have to be vetted and approved again.
Minority leader Mensah has asked the Supreme Court to rule on the matter. The court will hear the case on April 15.
In the meantime, sources close to the Castle expect the final cabinet to be known before the end of this week, when parliament goes into recess for Easter.
Rawlings's election victory, accepted by his opposition rivals, sent a strong democratic signal to would-be investors seeking stability.
But foreign businessmen say it is important to see how far Rawlings will embrace the more business-oriented policies of his main oppositon rival, lawyer-businessman John Kufuor.

Rawlings, who first seized power in 1979 and then in 1981 after a brief but chaotic period of civilian government, switched from socialist beginnings to World Bank-sponored free-market structural reform.

But World Bank and independent economists say Ghana, once hailed by the Bank as a model pupil, took a wrong turn before the 1992 elections when Rawlings decided to give its army of civil servants an 80 percent pay increase it could not afford.
The economy, they say, is still paying the price.
